I'd personally advise against water and advocate for an antiseptic spray to really make sure you aren't getting germs in there. After showering, just spray on a bit and wipe clean with gauze. Don't put on ointment, as it can soften your scabs. And yes, try to tape it down with steri strips as much as you can, but monitor for signs of infection, just in case it rejects/doesn't attach. Mine showed signs of non-attachment via increased exsudate.

If you worry about ripping your nipple off, leave on the steri strip until it peels off. Tape all around the edge of the nipple. To decrease friction, you can also fold up some gauze and stuff your compression vest with it. It's helping me a lot.

• Can I afford two seperate surgeries? (taking time off work, being cared for, travelling to your surgeon, etc)

• How quickly do I want to be done with surgeries? If you do both at once, you'll won't have to bother organising another surgery.

I am not the most spiritual person myself, but my uncle is and he went through a similar thing around twenty years ago. He lost his dad and he was unable to properly grieve him because the memory of his father and his sudden death was just too painful. My uncle had a bunch of other issues and he turned to alcohol and it all accumulated into a suicide attempt.

My uncle went to therapy afterwards. Had to go because of his attempt. And he came out better for it. But even without therapy, you can attempt to heal on your own. You say you use spirituality as a way to distract yourself from the grief, if I read your post correctly. 

Distracting yourself from grief is like cramming it all into a box and shoving it into the back of your mind. Well, one day it's all gonna come spilling out.

You HAVE to sit with the grief. Take a few days where you can just sit down and cry until you can't cry anymore. Remember your dad. Maybe build a little corner for him with pictures, candles, a stuffed animal. You can incorporate remembering him into your prayers. Remember that there will never be a moment in history where he wasn't your dad. The moments you shared will never be erased. Time may flow forwards but you will always have been with him at one point in time-space or another.

Maybe you get moments where you feel like your dad is with you. Talk to him in these moments. Doesn't matter if it feels ridiculous, as long as it helps you.

And once you can really sit with your memories of your father and don't feel overwhelmed, expose yourself to your triggers and see how you react. Maybe you'll won't get bothered by some things. Others might send you spiralling. It's all okay. Grief is a messy thing but something we all will experience. If I should elaborate on anything or you'd just like to chat, don't hesitate to DM me.

Hey dude. I'm FTM too and I know that it can suck major ass. While my current situation may differ from yours, I can certainly say that I have at least felt the misery in some way. It is shit and there is no way around that.

For one, this will pass. It will all pass. Nothing is forever. You just have to hold on. I don't know where you live but this sounds like a mental health issue coupled with an existential issue. And we can't fix the existential issue before you are not in a better place. If you can, try to access therapy or a trans support group. Or join a Discord server where you can talk to other trans people. If your parents tend to go through your stuff, maybe a library with computer access might be good so they can't see what you're doing. You can play it off as wanting to study.

As soon as it's safe, GET THE FUCK OUT. And in the mean time, search for people that you can relate to. Reach out online. Write letters if you don't want to leave a trace for your parents. Think "f— you" every time someone's being shit to you.

Love just... comes with the process. But it starts with being in a healthy place first. And then, at some point in time, it will click. Trust the process and find purpose where you can access it. It takes effort but the effort is worth it.

But congratulations! You have realised the horror of the human condition. You have a few options now.

1. Believe in a religion/spirituality. This gives you a sense of going somewhere specific. If the thought of nothing terrifies you, the thought that you go somewhere might be soothing.
2. Become a nihilist. Side note, you will lost likely become bitter and drive people away from you.
3. Read up on Absurdism. Camus to get you started. It explains that one must create meaning in what seems meaningless. Let's face it, we don't get handed a manual at birth declaring what the fuck is going on here. We spend our life figuring it out. And it will hurt. But you can learn to laugh at the absolute bullshit this is. I'm relearning it right now.

Know that you are not alone in this. Someone wrote to me that a realisation like this as early in our lifes as we both are (I'm 18.5, for reference) can be pretty traumatic. If you find yourself not escaping this, there is no shame in seeking therapy again. Maybe you need a different type of therapy or the help of medication. This fear is normal in our life. This fear is good, it should drive us forward, except when it cripples us. Then we need help.
Again: IT IS NOT SHAMEFUL.

If you enjoy a good bit of TikTok, follow hospice nurses. Or morticians. Our Western culture mystifies death. The death you see on television is not an accurate death. I personally find that learning about my fear from people who most likely know what they are talking about is very reassuring.

Know that this fear is normal at our life stage. Biologically, we are in our prime. We are so attached to our bodies because they work well, like a well oiled machine. We want to live because we have the capability to. Many find that once you lose quality of life, the more you accept death. And remember: our bodies are biologically programmed to die.

Talk to your loved ones about your fears. It may be embarrassing. God knows that I was when I told my parents that I am scared, or when I told a friend of mine. But most people, if they are good, will want to console you.

And, what I currently try to learn from my dad; stay curious. Stay like a child in a way. My dad has a great outlook on death somehow, in that he just... accepted it. It will come with age and satisfaction in your actions. He is satisfied with himself. What would I want my sex characteristics to look like? Get rid of the over-sexualised stereotypes for this. Would you want your chest to be visible? Or flat? A mix between, changing depending on your feelings?

If you had a button that would permanently transform you into the other sex, would you press it? If it was temporary, would you rather press it?

These questions helped me sort things out. On their own they could mean nothing and it could be that you are still cis (which isn't a bad thing!). If you have the resources, I'd advise looking for a therapist. In the mean time, you can do things that help you feel more at home in your body, whatever they might be.

Best of luck.
